## Introduction

Part 5 left the PGARCH branch open but unresolved. The three-channel `PGARCH-L` decomposition improved QLIKE relative to the earlier STES family and directionally improved on `GARCH(1,1)`, but it did not clear the series decision rule on its own. At the same time, the earlier feature-expansion work showed that simply widening the predictor set inside a single STES gate was not enough to create a useful forecasting gain.

Part 6 sits between that simpler PGARCH result and the broader Part 7 search. Its role is narrower than a final model-selection post. This is the step where the PGARCH line is expanded beyond the Part 5 formulations and asked a specific question: if the predictor set is made materially richer, does the predictive-GARCH recursion improve once those predictors are allowed to affect different structural channels rather than one common gate?

The answer in this notebook is disciplined but mixed. The all-feature linear PGARCH variants do not beat the Part 5 `PGARCH-L` baseline, and none of the expanded linear variants clears `GARCH(1,1)` under the Part 6 protocol. That negative result matters. It shows that richer information alone is not enough. At the same time, the exercise clarifies where richer predictors plausibly belong inside the recursion, exposes the limits of regularization-only allocation, and identifies the nonlinear XGBPGARCH line as the natural next search step rather than a solved endpoint.

The notebook therefore does four things in sequence. It places Part 6 inside the series, lays out the channel-based model roadmap and evaluation standard, summarizes the forecasting evidence, and then reads the diagnostic results that motivate Part 7.

## Why Part 6 Exists

This post is the expansion step inside the PGARCH branch of the series. Part 5 worked with a small return-based feature set and asked whether the predictive-GARCH decomposition itself helped. Part 6 keeps the dataset, target, benchmark, and train/test protocol fixed, but expands the PGARCH line along a different axis: richer predictors and richer allocation across the level $\mu_t$, persistence $\phi_t$, and innovation-share $g_t$ channels.

That placement matters for interpretation. Part 6 is not meant to settle the full expanded-feature problem. It is an intermediate result. The goal is to see whether a more structured linear PGARCH specification can turn the earlier feature-expansion idea into a benchmark-relevant forecasting gain, or whether the branch still needs a broader search over feature compression, nonlinear channel updates, or both.

The right public reading is therefore conservative. A positive finding here would mean that the expanded PGARCH line remains active under the Part 6 protocol. A negative finding would still be useful if it clarified which types of richer structure were worth carrying into Part 7.

## Model Roadmap

### The PGARCH Recursion

The PGARCH model defines the one-step-ahead variance forecast as

$$
h_{t+1} = (1 - \phi_t)\,\mu_t + \phi_t\,q_t, \qquad q_t = g_t\,y_t + (1 - g_t)\,h_t
$$

where $y_t \ge 0$ is the realized target, $h_t$ is the current variance forecast, and the three structural parameters are interpreted as follows. The level channel $\mu_t$ sets the anchor toward which variance mean-reverts. The persistence channel $\phi_t$ controls how strongly the recursion leans on that anchor versus the internal update. The innovation-share channel $g_t$ controls how aggressively new information is absorbed into the recursion.

In `PGARCH-L`, each channel is a linear function of predictors passed through a link that enforces admissible values:

$$
\mu_t = \mu_{\min} + \text{softplus}(\tilde{x}_{t-1}^\top w_\mu), \qquad
\phi_t = \phi_{\min} + (\phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min})\,\sigma(\tilde{x}_{t-1}^\top w_\phi), \qquad
g_t = g_{\min} + (g_{\max} - g_{\min})\,\sigma(\tilde{x}_{t-1}^\top w_g)
$$

The important modeling detail for Part 6 is that the current `PGARCHLinearModel` passes the same feature matrix to all three channels. Differential shrinkage is therefore a disciplined first attempt at channel allocation, not a hard architectural separation.

### The Part 6 Ladder

The progression into the Part 6 models is simple and deliberate.

| Step | Model | What changes | Why it is in scope |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | Linear `PGARCH-L` baseline | Reuse the Part 5 three-feature specification | Anchor the expanded-feature experiment to the accepted family baseline |
| 2 | Expanded linear PGARCH with uniform shrinkage | Pass the richer feature matrix to all channels with common penalties | Test whether more predictors help at all |
| 3 | Expanded linear PGARCH with channel-specific shrinkage | Keep the richer feature matrix, but vary `lambda_mu`, `lambda_phi`, and `lambda_g` | Test whether richer features help only when the channels are treated differently |
| 4 | Full `XGBPGARCHModel` preview | Replace linear channel maps with boosted updates in $\mu$, $\phi$, and $g$ | Check whether the natural next step is a nonlinear channel update rather than another minor linear tweak |

This roadmap separates three questions that are easy to blur together. The first is whether linear PGARCH benefits from broader information at all. The second is whether channel-specific allocation helps more than uniform expansion. The third is whether a boosted or nonlinear update becomes the right next branch once the linear expanded models stall.

## Feature Universe and Taxonomy

The executable Part 6 snapshot contains a 54-column predictor matrix. It reuses the broader feature-engineering ideas developed earlier in the series, but the realized design in this notebook is the 54-column matrix produced by the Part 6 pipeline and local data availability.

The taxonomy below is organizational rather than architectural. In the current linear PGARCH implementation, every feature is passed to every channel. The taxonomy simply records which channel a feature class is most naturally associated with before shrinkage is applied.

Fast return and intraday measures are the natural candidates for $g_t$. Volatility-state variables such as HAR-style realized-volatility summaries, downside asymmetry, and volatility-of-volatility are the natural candidates for $\phi_t$. Slower state variables such as implied-volatility levels, cross-asset conditions, macro-release timing, and liquidity controls are most naturally associated with $\mu_t$.

That distinction is important for how the evidence should be read. The allocation table below is a prior about intended use, not proof that the fitted model enforces that allocation cleanly. One of the Part 6 findings is that shrinkage alone only partially succeeds at that task.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Build expanded feature set (adapted from feature expansion notebook)

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Feature construction pipeline, adapted from the STES/XGBSTES feature expansion
# notebook (posts/volatility-forecasts-7/draft.ipynb).  We reuse the same
# engineering logic to ensure consistency across the series.
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# ── Shared OHLCV data ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ohlcv = sample_cached.set_index("date")[["open", "close", "volume"]].copy()
ohlcv.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(ohlcv.index)
ohlcv = ohlcv.sort_index()
ohlcv_aligned = ohlcv.reindex(target_idx, method="ffill")

# ── 1. Intraday return decomposition ─────────────────────────────────────────
intra_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
prev_close = ohlcv_aligned["close"].shift(1)
intra_df["overnight_return"] = np.log(ohlcv_aligned["open"] / prev_close)
intra_df["intraday_return"] = np.log(ohlcv_aligned["close"] / ohlcv_aligned["open"])
intra_df["overnight_sq"] = intra_df["overnight_return"] ** 2
intra_df["intraday_sq"] = intra_df["intraday_return"] ** 2
intra_df = intra_df.fillna(0.0)
intraday_cols = list(intra_df.columns)

# ── 2. HAR multi-horizon realised volatility ─────────────────────────────────
rv_daily = r_par ** 2
har_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
har_df["rv_1"] = rv_daily.shift(1)
har_df["rv_5"] = rv_daily.rolling(5, min_periods=1).mean().shift(1)
har_df["rv_22"] = rv_daily.rolling(22, min_periods=1).mean().shift(1)
har_df["rv_60"] = rv_daily.rolling(60, min_periods=1).mean().shift(1)
har_df["rv_ratio_5_22"] = har_df["rv_5"] / har_df["rv_22"].clip(lower=1e-12)
har_df = har_df.fillna(0.0)
har_rv_cols = list(har_df.columns)

# ── 3. Downside asymmetry and leverage effect ────────────────────────────────
neg_mask = (r_par < 0).astype(float)
pos_mask = (r_par >= 0).astype(float)
rv_daily_asym = r_par ** 2

asym_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
neg_rv = (rv_daily_asym * neg_mask).rolling(22, min_periods=1).sum().shift(1)
pos_rv = (rv_daily_asym * pos_mask).rolling(22, min_periods=1).sum().shift(1)
asym_df["neg_semi_rv_22"] = neg_rv
asym_df["pos_neg_rv_ratio"] = pos_rv / neg_rv.clip(lower=1e-12)
asym_df["signed_rv_interaction"] = (r_par * rv_daily_asym).shift(1)
asym_df["downside_freq_22"] = neg_mask.rolling(22, min_periods=1).mean().shift(1)
asym_df = asym_df.fillna(0.0)
asym_cols = list(asym_df.columns)

# ── 4. Volatility-of-volatility and regime dispersion ────────────────────────
rv_daily_vov = r_par ** 2
vov_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
vov_df["vov_22"] = rv_daily_vov.rolling(22, min_periods=5).std().shift(1)
rv_max_22 = rv_daily_vov.rolling(22, min_periods=5).max().shift(1)
rv_min_22 = rv_daily_vov.rolling(22, min_periods=5).min().shift(1)
vov_df["rv_range_22"] = rv_max_22 - rv_min_22
rv_lag1 = rv_daily_vov.shift(1)
vov_df["rv_autocorr_5"] = rv_daily_vov.rolling(5, min_periods=3).corr(rv_lag1).shift(1)
vov_df = vov_df.fillna(0.0)
vov_cols = list(vov_df.columns)

# ── 5. Volume and liquidity ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
vol_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
spy_vol_aligned = ohlcv_aligned["volume"]
spy_close_aligned = ohlcv_aligned["close"]
vol_df["volume_ratio"] = spy_vol_aligned / spy_vol_aligned.rolling(20, min_periods=1).mean()
dollar_volume = spy_close_aligned * spy_vol_aligned
vol_df["amihud_illiq"] = (r_par.abs() / dollar_volume) * 1e6
vol_df = vol_df.fillna(0.0)
volume_cols = list(vol_df.columns)

# ── 6. Calendar and event features ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Deterministic features — no API needed, computed from the trading calendar
try:
    from alphaforge.features import CalendarFlagsTemplate, EventDateTemplate
    from alphaforge.features.template import SliceSpec as AFSliceSpec

    cal_tmpl = CalendarFlagsTemplate()
    cal_slice = AFSliceSpec(start=SAMPLE_START, end=SAMPLE_END, entities=[SAMPLE_TICKER])
    cal_ff = cal_tmpl.transform(
        ctx_sample,
        params={
            "calendar": "XNYS",
            "flags": ("dow", "is_month_end", "is_quarter_end", "is_year_end"),
            "one_hot_dow": True,
        },
        slice=cal_slice,
        state=None,
    )
    if isinstance(cal_ff.index, pd.MultiIndex):
        cal_ff = cal_ff.xs(SAMPLE_TICKER, level="entity_id")
    cal_ff = cal_ff.reindex(target_idx).fillna(0.0)

    evt_tmpl = EventDateTemplate()
    evt_ff = evt_tmpl.transform(
        ctx_sample,
        params={
            "calendar": "XNYS",
            "events": ("fomc", "opex", "imm"),
            "near_window": 3,
        },
        slice=cal_slice,
        state=None,
    )
    if isinstance(evt_ff.index, pd.MultiIndex):
        evt_ff = evt_ff.xs(SAMPLE_TICKER, level="entity_id")
    evt_ff = evt_ff.reindex(target_idx).fillna(0.0)

    seasonal_df = pd.concat([cal_ff, evt_ff], axis=1)
    # Add period-end lead windows
    for col_end in ["is_month_end", "is_quarter_end", "is_year_end"]:
        if col_end in seasonal_df.columns:
            lead_col = col_end.replace("is_", "pre_") + "_3d"
            end_positions = seasonal_df[col_end] == 1
            lead_series = pd.Series(0.0, index=target_idx)
            for idx_pos in end_positions[end_positions].index:
                loc = target_idx.get_loc(idx_pos)
                for lag in range(1, 4):
                    if loc - lag >= 0:
                        lead_series.iloc[loc - lag] = 1.0
            seasonal_df[lead_col] = lead_series
    seasonal_cols = list(seasonal_df.columns)
    _cal_ok = True
    print(f"Calendar/event features: {len(seasonal_cols)} columns")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Calendar features unavailable ({e}); building minimal DOW flags")
    seasonal_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
    dow = target_idx.dayofweek
    for d in range(5):
        seasonal_df[f"dow_{d}"] = (dow == d).astype(float)
    seasonal_cols = list(seasonal_df.columns)
    _cal_ok = False

# ── 7. FRED-based features (VIX, cross-asset, stress, macro) ─────────────────
_fred_ok = False
fred_feature_dfs = []
fred_feature_cols = []
try:
    from fredapi import Fred
    fred = Fred(api_key=os.environ["FRED_API_KEY"])
    _start = SAMPLE_START.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    _end = SAMPLE_END.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

    def _fred_to_daily(s, col_name, tidx):
        s = s.rename(col_name)
        s.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(s.index)
        if tidx.tz is not None:
            s.index = s.index.tz_localize("UTC") if s.index.tz is None else s.index.tz_convert("UTC")
        else:
            s.index = s.index.tz_localize(None) if s.index.tz is not None else s.index
        return s.reindex(tidx, method="ffill")

    # VIX features
    vix_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
    vix_series = fred.get_series("VIXCLS", observation_start=_start, observation_end=_end).dropna()
    vix_df["vix_level"] = _fred_to_daily(vix_series, "vix_level", target_idx)
    vix_df["vix_change"] = vix_df["vix_level"].diff().fillna(0.0)
    vix_df["vix_level"] = vix_df["vix_level"].ffill().bfill()
    try:
        vix3m = fred.get_series("VXVCLS", observation_start=_start, observation_end=_end).dropna()
        vix_df["vix_term_slope"] = _fred_to_daily(vix_series, "v1", target_idx) - _fred_to_daily(vix3m, "v2", target_idx)
        vix_df["vix3m_available"] = _fred_to_daily(vix3m, "v3", target_idx).notna().astype(float)
    except Exception:
        vix_df["vix_term_slope"] = 0.0
        vix_df["vix3m_available"] = 0.0
    # IV-RV spread
    rv_20_annualised = np.sqrt(rv_daily.rolling(20, min_periods=5).mean().shift(1) * 252) * 100
    vix_df["iv_rv_spread"] = vix_df["vix_level"] - rv_20_annualised
    vix_df = vix_df.fillna(0.0)
    vix_cols = list(vix_df.columns)
    fred_feature_dfs.append(vix_df[vix_cols])

    # Cross-asset features
    cross_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
    fred_cross = {
        "BAMLH0A0HYM2": "credit_spread",
        "T10Y2Y": "curve_slope",
        "DCOILWTICO": "oil_price",
        "DGS2": "short_rate_level",
        "DGS10": "long_rate_level",
        "DTWEXBGS": "usd_level",
    }
    for fred_id, col_name in fred_cross.items():
        try:
            s = fred.get_series(fred_id, observation_start=_start, observation_end=_end).dropna()
            cross_df[col_name] = _fred_to_daily(s, col_name, target_idx)
        except Exception:
            cross_df[col_name] = np.nan

    try:
        copper_monthly = fred.get_series("PCOPPUSDM", observation_start=_start, observation_end=_end).dropna()
        cross_df["copper_level"] = _fred_to_daily(copper_monthly, "copper_level", target_idx)
    except Exception:
        cross_df["copper_level"] = np.nan

    try:
        gld_src = TiingoEODSource(api_key=os.environ.get("TIINGO_API") or os.environ.get("TIINGO_API_KEY"))
        gld_raw = gld_src.fetch(Query(
            table="market.ohlcv", columns=["close"],
            start=SAMPLE_START, end=SAMPLE_END, entities=["GLD"],
        ))
        gld_close = gld_raw.set_index("date")["close"].rename("gold_price")
        if target_idx.tz is None:
            gld_close.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(gld_close.index).tz_localize(None)
        else:
            gld_close.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(gld_close.index).tz_convert(target_idx.tz)
        cross_df["gold_price"] = gld_close.reindex(target_idx, method="ffill")
    except Exception:
        cross_df["gold_price"] = np.nan

    # Derived
    cross_df["gold_return"] = np.log(cross_df["gold_price"] / cross_df["gold_price"].shift(1))
    cross_df["oil_return"] = np.log(cross_df["oil_price"] / cross_df["oil_price"].shift(1))
    cross_df["copper_change"] = cross_df["copper_level"].pct_change()
    cross_df["short_rate_change"] = cross_df["short_rate_level"].diff()
    cross_df["long_rate_change"] = cross_df["long_rate_level"].diff()
    cross_df["usd_change"] = cross_df["usd_level"].pct_change()
    cross_df["usd_available"] = cross_df["usd_level"].notna().astype(float)

    for col in ["credit_spread", "curve_slope", "short_rate_level", "long_rate_level",
                 "usd_level", "copper_level"]:
        cross_df[col] = cross_df[col].ffill().bfill()
    for col in ["gold_return", "oil_return", "copper_change",
                 "short_rate_change", "long_rate_change", "usd_change"]:
        cross_df[col] = cross_df[col].fillna(0.0)
    cross_df["usd_level"] = cross_df["usd_level"].ffill().bfill()
    cross_df = cross_df.drop(columns=["oil_price", "gold_price"], errors="ignore")
    cross_asset_cols = [c for c in cross_df.columns if c not in ("oil_price", "gold_price")]
    cross_df = cross_df[cross_asset_cols].fillna(0.0)
    fred_feature_dfs.append(cross_df)

    # Financial stress
    stress_df = pd.DataFrame(index=target_idx)
    stress_series = {
        "VVIXCLS": "vvix_level",
        "NFCI": "nfci_level",
        "STLFSI4": "stlfsi_level",
        "TEDRATE": "ted_spread",
    }
    for fred_id, col_name in stress_series.items():
        try:
            s = fred.get_series(fred_id, observation_start=_start, observation_end=_end).dropna()
            stress_df[col_name] = _fred_to_daily(s, col_name, target_idx)
        except Exception:
            stress_df[col_name] = np.nan
    stress_df = stress_df.ffill().bfill().fillna(0.0)
    stress_cols = list(stress_df.columns)
    fred_feature_dfs.append(stress_df)

    # Macro release dates
    macro_df = pd.DataFrame(0.0, index=target_idx, columns=[])
    trading_dates = target_idx
    macro_release_series = {"gdp": "GDP", "cpi": "CPIAUCSL", "nfp": "PAYEMS"}
    for label, fred_id in macro_release_series.items():
        try:
            vintages = fred.get_series_vintage_dates(fred_id)
            release_dates = pd.DatetimeIndex(vintages)
            if trading_dates.tz is not None:
                release_dates = release_dates.tz_localize("UTC") if release_dates.tz is None else release_dates.tz_convert("UTC")
            else:
                release_dates = release_dates.tz_localize(None) if release_dates.tz is not None else release_dates
            release_dates = release_dates.normalize()
            macro_df[f"is_{label}_release"] = trading_dates.isin(release_dates).astype(float)
            # Pre-release 1d indicator (aligned to forecast date t+1)
            pre_col = f"pre_{label}_1d"
            shifted_releases = release_dates - pd.tseries.offsets.BDay(1)
            macro_df[pre_col] = trading_dates.isin(shifted_releases).astype(float)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  Macro release {label} unavailable: {e}")
            macro_df[f"is_{label}_release"] = 0.0
            macro_df[f"pre_{label}_1d"] = 0.0
    macro_cols = list(macro_df.columns)
    fred_feature_dfs.append(macro_df)

    _fred_ok = True
    for _df in fred_feature_dfs:
        fred_feature_cols.extend(list(_df.columns))
    print(f"FRED-based features: {len(fred_feature_cols)} columns")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"FRED features unavailable ({e}); proceeding without them")
    _fred_ok = False

# ── Assemble the expanded feature matrix ─────────────────────────────────────
# Start with the baseline return features (no const)
expanded_parts = [X_par[base_feat_cols]]

# Return-derived features (always available)
expanded_parts.extend([intra_df, har_df, asym_df, vov_df, vol_df])

# Calendar features (usually available)
expanded_parts.append(seasonal_df)

# FRED features (if available)
if _fred_ok:
    expanded_parts.extend(fred_feature_dfs)

X_expanded = pd.concat(expanded_parts, axis=1)
X_expanded = X_expanded.fillna(0.0)

# Remove any duplicate columns
X_expanded = X_expanded.loc[:, ~X_expanded.columns.duplicated()]

expanded_feat_cols = list(X_expanded.columns)

# Split
X_exp_tr = X_expanded.iloc[SAMPLE_TRAIN_START:SAMPLE_SPLIT_INDEX]
X_exp_te = X_expanded.iloc[SAMPLE_SPLIT_INDEX:]
X_exp_all = pd.concat([X_exp_tr, X_exp_te])

print(f"\nExpanded feature matrix: {X_expanded.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Return-based:       {len(base_feat_cols)}")
print(f"  Intraday decomp:    {len(intraday_cols)}")
print(f"  HAR-RV:             {len(har_rv_cols)}")
print(f"  Asymmetry:          {len(asym_cols)}")
print(f"  Vol-of-vol:         {len(vov_cols)}")
print(f"  Volume/liquidity:   {len(volume_cols)}")
print(f"  Calendar/event:     {len(seasonal_cols)}")
if _fred_ok:
    print(f"  FRED-based:         {len(fred_feature_cols)}")
print(f"  Train: {X_exp_tr.shape}, Test: {X_exp_te.shape}")
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Feature allocation taxonomy

def _assign_channel(feat_name):
    '''Assign a primary PGARCH channel based on the feature economic role.'''
    f = feat_name.lower()

    # g-channel: fast shock features
    g_features = {"overnight_return", "intraday_return", "overnight_sq", "intraday_sq",
                   "signed_rv_interaction"}
    if f in g_features:
        return "g (innovation)"
    if any(k in f for k in ["logret", "log_return"]):
        return "g (innovation)"

    # phi-channel: persistence features
    phi_features = {"rv_autocorr_5", "vov_22", "rv_range_22", "rv_ratio_5_22",
                    "neg_semi_rv_22", "pos_neg_rv_ratio", "downside_freq_22",
                    "rv_5", "rv_22", "rv_60", "rv_1"}
    if f in phi_features:
        return "phi (persistence)"

    # Everything else -> mu-channel
    return "mu (level)"


def _assign_group(feat_name):
    '''Assign a feature group label.'''
    f = feat_name.lower()
    if any(k in f for k in ["logret", "log_return"]):
        return "Return-based"
    if f.startswith("dow_"):
        return "Calendar (DOW)"
    if any(k in f for k in ["month_end", "quarter_end", "year_end"]):
        return "Calendar (Period-end)"
    if any(k in f for k in ["fomc", "opex", "imm"]):
        return "Calendar (Events)"
    if any(k in f for k in ["vix", "iv_rv", "vix3m"]):
        return "VIX / Implied Vol"
    if any(k in f for k in ["credit", "curve", "gold", "oil", "rate", "usd", "copper"]):
        return "Cross-Asset"
    if any(k in f for k in ["volume", "amihud"]):
        return "Volume / Liquidity"
    if any(k in f for k in ["gdp", "cpi", "nfp"]):
        return "Macro Release"
    if any(k in f for k in ["overnight", "intraday"]):
        return "Intraday Decomp"
    if any(k in f for k in ["rv_", "neg_semi", "downside", "signed_rv",
                             "vov_", "nfci", "stlfsi", "ted", "vvix"]):
        return "Volatility State"
    return "Other"


taxonomy = pd.DataFrame({
    "Feature": expanded_feat_cols,
    "Group": [_assign_group(f) for f in expanded_feat_cols],
    "Channel": [_assign_channel(f) for f in expanded_feat_cols],
})

channel_summary = taxonomy.groupby("Channel")["Feature"].count().rename("Count")
group_summary = taxonomy.groupby(["Channel", "Group"])["Feature"].count().rename("Count")
print("Channel allocation summary:")
print(channel_summary.to_string())
print()
print("Detailed group × channel:")
print(group_summary.to_string())

display(style_results_table(taxonomy, precision=0, index_col="Feature"))
```

## Evaluation Standard and Experimental Design

The dataset, target, and split are held fixed relative to Part 5. After the 200-row warm-up discard, the effective sample contains 3,800 training observations and 2,035 out-of-sample observations on SPY daily variance from 2000 through 2023. `GARCH(1,1)` remains the benchmark, and the Part 5 `PGARCH-L` baseline remains the active family reference.

The underlying model implementations live in the sibling `volatility-forecast` repository, principally `volatility_forecast/model/pgarch_linear_model.py` for the linear branch and `volatility_forecast/model/xgb_pgarch_full_model.py` for the nonlinear preview.

### What Counts as Success

This series is not selecting models by in-sample fit. The decision rule remains the same as in Part 4 and Part 5: lower out-of-sample QLIKE than `GARCH(1,1)`, with Diebold-Mariano tests on QLIKE loss used to judge whether a benchmark improvement is statistically credible. RMSE and in-sample QLIKE remain useful diagnostics, but they are secondary. A model that fits the training window better while losing on OS QLIKE or failing against the benchmark is not treated as a success.

### Part 6 Variants

We define five linear PGARCH variants that move one step at a time through the expanded-feature question.

| Model | Features | `lambda_mu` | `lambda_phi` | `lambda_g` | Design intent |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **A** - Part 5 baseline | 3 return features | 0 | 0 | 0 | Reproduce the accepted Part 5 `PGARCH-L` reference |
| **B** - Expanded, uniform | All expanded | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.01 | Ask whether all-feature linear expansion helps at all |
| **C** - Structured, rich `mu` | All expanded | 0.001 | 0.01 | 0.1 | Test the main channel-allocation idea |
| **D** - Structured, very rich `mu` | All expanded | 0.0001 | 0.01 | 0.1 | Check whether giving the level channel even more freedom helps or overfits |
| **E** - Structured, relaxed `g` | All expanded | 0.001 | 0.01 | 0.01 | Check whether the innovation channel benefits from broader access |

The key comparisons are therefore easy to state. Model B against Model A asks whether simple expansion helps. Model C against Model B asks whether channel-specific shrinkage helps more than uniform shrinkage. Model D against Model C asks whether extra freedom in the level channel is useful or just costly. Model E against Model C asks whether a lean `g` channel is a helpful prior or an unnecessary restriction.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Fit GARCH(1,1) baseline

r_tr_pct = r_tr * SCALE_FACTOR
r_all_concat = pd.concat([r_tr, r_te])
r_all_pct = r_all_concat * SCALE_FACTOR

garch_spec = arch_model(r_tr_pct, vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1, mean="Zero", rescale=False)
garch_fit = garch_spec.fit(disp="off")
omega_g, alpha_g, beta_g = (
    garch_fit.params["omega"],
    garch_fit.params["alpha[1]"],
    garch_fit.params["beta[1]"],
)

cv_sq_is = garch_fit.conditional_volatility.values ** 2
r_sq_is = r_tr_pct.values ** 2
garch_pred_is = (omega_g + alpha_g * r_sq_is + beta_g * cv_sq_is) / (SCALE_FACTOR ** 2)

garch_spec_full = arch_model(r_all_pct, vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1, mean="Zero", rescale=False)
garch_fit_full = garch_spec_full.fit(disp="off", last_obs=len(r_tr))
garch_fcast = garch_fit_full.forecast(start=len(r_tr), reindex=False)
garch_pred_os = garch_fcast.variance.values.flatten() / (SCALE_FACTOR ** 2)

print(f"GARCH(1,1): omega={omega_g:.6f}, alpha={alpha_g:.4f}, beta={beta_g:.4f}")
```

## Main Results Summary

The full metric table above is the detailed record. The compact summary below is the reading guide for the rest of the post.

| Model | OS QLIKE | DM vs GARCH (QLIKE) | p-value | Part 6 reading |
|:---|---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| `GARCH(1,1)` | `1.561044` | `0.0000` | `-` | benchmark |
| `A: PGARCH-L baseline` | `1.550144` | not re-tabulated here | not re-tabulated here | improves on mean OS QLIKE, but remains a carry-over non-significant benchmark comparison from Part 5 |
| `B: Expanded uniform` | `1.604755` | not re-tabulated here | not re-tabulated here | negative result |
| `C: Structured (rich mu)` | `1.625556` | `1.5542` | `0.1203` | negative result |
| `D: Structured (very rich mu)` | `1.830423` | not re-tabulated here | not re-tabulated here | negative result |
| `E: Structured (relaxed g)` | `1.616961` | not re-tabulated here | not re-tabulated here | negative result |
| `XGBPGARCHModel` preview | fit failed | initializer failure | `-` | unresolved preview |

The headline result is straightforward. The Part 5 three-feature `PGARCH-L` baseline remains the strongest forecast inside this notebook. The expanded linear models all improve in-sample fit, but those gains do not survive out of sample. Part 6 therefore adds structure and diagnostics more clearly than it adds predictive performance.

## Statistical Comparison

Point rankings are not enough on their own. The Diebold-Mariano table below checks whether the visible QLIKE differences are large enough to treat as more than noise.

In this notebook the DM evidence mostly reinforces, rather than overturns, the ranking table. The expanded all-feature models are not merely failing to post a benchmark-clearing p-value. On the most important comparisons, the loss differentials also point in the wrong direction.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Diebold-Mariano tests

def _qlike_loss(y, yhat):
    y_a, h_a = np.asarray(y, float), np.maximum(np.asarray(yhat, float), 1e-12)
    return np.log(h_a) + y_a / h_a

def _sq_loss(y, yhat):
    return (np.asarray(y, float) - np.asarray(yhat, float)) ** 2

dm_pairs = [
    ("C: Structured (rich mu)", "GARCH(1,1)"),
    ("C: Structured (rich mu)", "A: PGARCH-L baseline"),
    ("C: Structured (rich mu)", "B: Expanded uniform"),
    ("C: Structured (rich mu)", "E: Structured (relaxed g)"),
    ("D: Structured (very rich mu)", "C: Structured (rich mu)"),
    ("B: Expanded uniform", "A: PGARCH-L baseline"),
]

dm_rows = []
for loss_name, loss_fn in [("QLIKE", _qlike_loss), ("Squared", _sq_loss)]:
    for name_a, name_b in dm_pairs:
        _, pred_a = model_predictions[name_a]
        _, pred_b = model_predictions[name_b]
        loss_a = loss_fn(actual_os, pred_a)
        loss_b = loss_fn(actual_os, pred_b)
        dm_result = diebold_mariano(loss_a, loss_b)
        dm_rows.append({
            "Loss": loss_name,
            "Model A": name_a,
            "Model B": name_b,
            "DM stat": dm_result["dm_stat"],
            "p-value": dm_result["p_value"],
            "Mean diff": dm_result["mean_d"],
        })

dm_df = pd.DataFrame(dm_rows)
display(style_results_table(dm_df, precision=4, index_col="Model A"))
```

### Reading the DM Tests

Three comparisons carry most of the interpretive weight.

First, Model C is worse than `GARCH(1,1)` on mean OS QLIKE, and its DM statistic against `GARCH(1,1)` is `1.5542` with `p = 0.1203`. That is not a benchmark-clearing result.

Second, Model C is worse than the Part 5 `PGARCH-L` baseline, and that comparison is stronger. The DM statistic against Model A is `1.9879` with `p = 0.0470`. The first structured all-feature specification is therefore not just inconclusive against the benchmark; it is materially worse than the simpler three-feature baseline under the Part 6 protocol.

Third, making the `mu` channel even looser is a negative result rather than an improvement. Model D is worse than Model C, with DM statistic `2.6157` and `p = 0.0090`. In this all-feature linear setup, extra freedom in the level channel amplifies overfitting rather than uncovering additional predictive signal.

The remaining rows are still useful. Uniform regularization does not improve on the Part 5 baseline, and relaxing the `g` penalty does not rescue the expanded design. The expanded linear branch therefore remains active as a modeling question, but not yet as a benchmark-clearing forecasting result.

## Channel Diagnostics

The diagnostic plots do not overturn the forecasting result, but they explain why the structured branch remained worth carrying forward. PGARCH is useful here because it reveals how the richer feature set changes the level anchor, persistence, and innovation share even when headline OS performance does not improve.

The question in this section is therefore diagnostic rather than promotional. Do the expanded models move the channels in economically interpretable ways, and do those movements help explain both the promise and the failure of the Part 6 specifications?

## Coefficient and Allocation Diagnostics

Coefficient inspection is useful here as a diagnostic, not as a victory lap. The question is whether differential shrinkage actually steers features toward their intended roles, and whether any such steering is strong enough to support the structural story told in the setup section.

That is a stricter standard than simply finding large coefficients. A publication-ready reading has to ask whether the intended allocation is visible in the fitted weights, and whether the answer is strong enough to explain the forecasting outcomes.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Per-channel coefficient analysis for Model C

def _extract_channel_coefs(model, feat_cols):
    '''Extract per-channel coefficients (on the standardised scale).'''
    theta = model.theta_
    block = len(theta) // 3
    # First element of each block is the intercept
    w_mu = theta[:block]
    w_phi = theta[block:2*block]
    w_g = theta[2*block:]
    # Skip intercept (index 0)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "Feature": feat_cols,
        "Group": [_assign_group(f) for f in feat_cols],
        "Primary channel": [_assign_channel(f) for f in feat_cols],
        "w_mu": w_mu[1:],
        "w_phi": w_phi[1:],
        "w_g": w_g[1:],
        "|w_mu|": np.abs(w_mu[1:]),
        "|w_phi|": np.abs(w_phi[1:]),
        "|w_g|": np.abs(w_g[1:]),
    })


coef_df = _extract_channel_coefs(model_c, expanded_feat_cols)

# Top features per channel
for ch, label in [("mu", "mu (level)"), ("phi", "phi (persistence)"), ("g", "g (innovation)")]:
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Top 15 features in {label} channel (|w_{ch}|):")
    print(f"{'='*60}")
    top = coef_df.nlargest(15, f"|w_{ch}|")[["Feature", "Group", "Primary channel", f"w_{ch}", f"|w_{ch}|"]]
    print(top.to_string(index=False))
```

```{python}

coef_df["total_importance"] = coef_df["|w_mu|"] + coef_df["|w_phi|"] + coef_df["|w_g|"]
top20 = coef_df.nlargest(20, "total_importance")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 10))

im = ax.imshow(data_to_plot, cmap="RdBu_r", aspect="auto",
               vmin=-np.abs(data_to_plot).max(), vmax=np.abs(data_to_plot).max())

```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: 'Validate channel allocation: fraction of weight in primary vs other channels'

def _allocation_score(row):
    '''Fraction of total absolute weight in the primary channel.'''
    total = row["|w_mu|"] + row["|w_phi|"] + row["|w_g|"]
    if total < 1e-12:
        return np.nan
    ch_map = {"g (innovation)": "|w_g|", "phi (persistence)": "|w_phi|", "mu (level)": "|w_mu|"}
    primary_col = ch_map.get(row["Primary channel"], "|w_mu|")
    return row[primary_col] / total

coef_df["allocation_score"] = coef_df.apply(_allocation_score, axis=1)

# Group-level summary
alloc_summary = coef_df.groupby("Primary channel").agg(
    n_features=("Feature", "count"),
    mean_alloc=("allocation_score", "mean"),
    median_alloc=("allocation_score", "median"),
    mean_total_w=("total_importance", "mean"),
).round(4)

print("Allocation validation: fraction of weight in the intended channel")
print("(higher = regularisation is steering features as intended)\n")
display(style_results_table(alloc_summary, precision=4, index_col="Primary channel"))
```

The diagnostic evidence is mixed but informative. Relative to the Part 5 baseline, the structured models move more variation into the level and persistence channels and keep the $g_t$ path more stable when the $g$ penalty is kept high. But the allocation-score table also shows the limit of this approach: shrinkage alone does not produce a clean channel separation, especially for features intended for the innovation channel. The structural prior is only partially enforced, which helps explain why interpretability improved more than forecast accuracy.

## Nonlinear Preview and Boundary of Part 6

Part 6 includes only a boundary check on the full `XGBPGARCHModel`. It is not a Part 7-style model search. The purpose is narrower: if the all-feature linear PGARCH variants stall, is the natural next branch a boosted three-channel update rather than another minor linear reparameterization?

The answer from this notebook is provisional. The preview does not produce a usable nonlinear comparison because the default `linear_pgarch` initializer fails on the expanded design. That failure should not be read as evidence that the nonlinear branch loses. It should also not be read as a win. It shows that once the feature set is widened, the nonlinear PGARCH line already depends on initialization discipline before any substantive comparison can be made.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Fit full XGBPGARCHModel (optional — may be slow)

try:
    from volatility_forecast.model.xgb_pgarch_full_model import XGBPGARCHModel

    y_tr_scaled = y_tr.values * (SCALE_FACTOR ** 2)
    y_all_scaled = y_all.values * (SCALE_FACTOR ** 2)

    xgb_full = XGBPGARCHModel(
        loss="qlike",
        n_outer_rounds=25,
        trees_per_channel_per_round=1,
        learning_rate=0.02,
        max_depth=3,
        min_child_weight=5.0,
        reg_lambda=1.0,
        init_method="linear_pgarch",
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        verbosity=0,
    )
    xgb_full.fit(y_tr_scaled, X_exp_tr)
    h_xgb_full_scaled = xgb_full.predict_variance(y_all_scaled, X_exp_all)
    h_xgb_full = h_xgb_full_scaled / (SCALE_FACTOR ** 2)
    h_xgb_full_is = h_xgb_full[:len(y_tr)]
    h_xgb_full_os = h_xgb_full[len(y_tr):]

    xgb_full_rmse_os = rmse(actual_os, h_xgb_full_os)
    xgb_full_qlike_os = qlike(actual_os, h_xgb_full_os)
    print(f"XGBPGARCHModel (full): OS RMSE = {xgb_full_rmse_os:.6f}, OS QLIKE = {xgb_full_qlike_os:.6f}")

    # DM test vs Model C
    loss_xgb = _qlike_loss(actual_os, h_xgb_full_os)
    loss_c = _qlike_loss(actual_os, h_c_os)
    dm_xgb_vs_c = diebold_mariano(loss_xgb, loss_c)
    print(f"DM (XGBPGARCHModel vs Model C, QLIKE): stat={dm_xgb_vs_c['dm_stat']:.3f}, p={dm_xgb_vs_c['p_value']:.3f}")

    _xgb_full_available = True
except Exception as e:
    print(f"XGBPGARCHModel comparison skipped: {e}")
    _xgb_full_available = False
```

## What Part 6 Actually Learned

Part 6 leaves a cleaner result than the original draft suggested.

First, the Part 5 three-feature `PGARCH-L` baseline remains the strongest specification inside this notebook. It posts the best OS QLIKE among the evaluated fits.

Second, expanding the feature set inside linear PGARCH is not enough by itself. Models B through E all fit the training sample better than Model A, but each one loses ground out of sample. The Part 6 problem is therefore not lack of in-sample flexibility. It is controlling how richer information enters the recursion without paying too much variance.

Third, the structural story is still useful. The channel plots and coefficient tables indicate that richer predictors can move the level and persistence channels in economically interpretable ways, while the $g_t$ channel becomes much less stable when its penalty is relaxed. That is not a forecasting win, but it is enough to keep channel-specific modeling alive as an active branch at this stage of the series.

Fourth, the nonlinear extension remains unresolved rather than rejected. The full boosted preview fails at initialization, which identifies a concrete technical obstacle and a natural next search step.

## Limitations

The limitations are direct. Part 6 does not deliver an expanded-feature model that clears `GARCH(1,1)` on OS QLIKE. It also does not show that differential regularization alone can produce a clean channel allocation; the allocation-score table shows only partial steering, especially in the intended innovation channel. Finally, the nonlinear preview is incomplete because the initializer failed before a fair boosted comparison was available.

Those limitations are not incidental. They are the reason this post is an intermediate result rather than a final victory post.

## Handoff to Part 7

Part 7 is therefore the broader search-and-stress-test phase, not a retroactive correction to Part 6. Part 6 leaves the series with a live but unresolved branch: richer PGARCH specifications remain plausible, but the all-feature linear versions overfit and the first full nonlinear preview is blocked by initialization.

The natural next search step is to keep the benchmark, target, and QLIKE-based decision rule fixed while broadening the specification search inside the PGARCH and XGBPGARCH line. That means testing whether the encouraging ideas from Part 6 survive alternative feature allocations, narrower screened subsets, better initialization discipline, and stronger robustness checks. In that sense Part 7 extends Part 6 rather than overturning it. The question shifts from whether richer structure can help in principle to which richer structure, if any, survives a wider and stricter search.

## Appendix: Implied GARCH Parameters

For interpretability, we convert the structured PGARCH-L coefficients into implied $\omega_t = (1-\phi_t)\mu_t$, $\alpha_t = \phi_t g_t$, and $\beta_t = \phi_t(1-g_t)$ and report their test-period statistics.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Implied GARCH parameters for selected models

impl_rows = []
for label, (mod, X_mod) in models_to_plot.items():
    impl = mod.implied_garch_params(X_mod.values)
    for param in ["omega", "alpha", "beta"]:
        vals = impl[param]
        impl_rows.append({
            "Model": label,
            "Parameter": param,
            "Mean": np.mean(vals),
            "Std": np.std(vals),
            "Min": np.min(vals),
            "Max": np.max(vals),
        })

impl_df = pd.DataFrame(impl_rows)
display(style_results_table(impl_df, precision=6, index_col="Model"))

# Comparison with static GARCH(1,1)
print(f"\nStatic GARCH(1,1) parameters for reference:")
print(f"  omega = {omega_g:.6f}")
print(f"  alpha = {alpha_g:.4f}")
print(f"  beta  = {beta_g:.4f}")
```
